title: Comparative advantage
bridge: Trade allows two economies to mutually gain whenever their opportunity costs differ, but market equilibrium leaves the division of surplus entirely to relative size.
blurb: Two economies both gain at any price between their opportunity costs, but nobody gets to choose the price. Relative size sets it, both gain only inside a band exactly as wide as the gap between their costs, and an economy that is better at everything, trading with a partner its own size, can come away with exactly nothing.

title: Economic rent
bridge: Comparative advantage took production techniques as fixed endowments across nations. Economic rent investigates where technological differences originate: innovating firms adopt superior techniques to capture temporary rents, which competition systematically erodes while spreading the innovation.
blurb: Seven technologies make the same thing, and the rectangle test every first course teaches leaves five survivors — crowning a sensible middle option that is the cheapest choice at no price at all. Rent is the gap under the price, and competition closes it from below while copying the difference that opened it.

title: Supply and demand
bridge: Economic rent examined how technological differences open profit margins that competition subsequently erodes. Supply and demand investigates the market-level clearing mechanism itself, showing that price-quantity data identifies neither curve without exogenous supply shocks.
blurb: Price-quantity observations pin the true demand slope only to a bracket between direct and reverse regressions, and the bracket width ratio is exactly 1/R². The goodness-of-fit statistic is the identification failure read backwards: the better a naive line fits the cloud, the less it tells you about the curve.

title: Elasticity
bridge: Supply and demand showed how shifting curves trace out market equilibria, but took the slopes of those curves as given. Elasticity measures how quantities respond to price changes along any curve, revealing that responsiveness is geometrically identical to the ratio into which any point cuts its own tangent.
blurb: Price elasticity of demand is the ratio of the two segments into which a point divides its own tangent line: lower segment over upper segment. The geometric ruler holds exactly on every smooth demand curve, not just straight lines — revealing why elasticity varies continuously from zero to infinity along a constant slope.

title: Surplus and efficiency
bridge: Elasticity established how responsiveness varies along demand and supply curves. Surplus and efficiency integrates under those curves to measure the gains from trade, proving that non-price rationing inflicts first-order misallocation losses that dwarf the textbook deadweight loss triangle.
blurb: The textbook deadweight loss triangle scales as the square of the quantity cut, but random rationing under a price ceiling inflicts a first-order misallocation loss. In every linear market, the two channels sum to the quantity cut itself: d² + d(1 − d) = d. A 27% supply restriction destroys exactly 27% of the total gains from trade.

title: Tax incidence
bridge: Surplus and efficiency showed that market clearing maximises total surplus and identified the welfare losses from output cuts. Tax incidence introduces a government wedge between buyer price and seller price, proving that relative elasticities determine who actually bears the burden of the tax.
blurb: Who writes the cheque changes nothing, to fourteen decimal places; the elasticities set the split exactly for a straight line and only to first order otherwise — and at the revenue-maximising rate the tax has destroyed half the trades and burned half the take.

title: Cost curves
bridge: Tax incidence and market surplus treated supply curves as fixed marginal cost schedules without asking how firms produce. Cost curves opens the firm's production problem, showing that the long-run cost envelope touches short-run average cost at its minimum at exactly one plant size, and on its slope everywhere else.
blurb: The plant built for an output is run at its own cheapest scale at exactly one output, where the envelope tangency coincides with the short-run minimum. Everywhere else the envelope touches the curve on its slope, and the cost penalty of being forced to operate off-capacity is strictly second-order in the forecast error.

title: Perfect competition
bridge: Cost curves derived the cost envelope for an individual firm with flexible plant scale. Perfect competition aggregates whole numbers of identical firms into an industry, revealing that the integer constraint turns the smooth textbook supply curve into a persistent sawtooth.
blurb: Free entry cannot drive price down to minimum average cost because firms are discrete whole numbers. Surviving profit is (1 + x)² − 1 fixed costs with x = frac(n̄)/(Bd + n*), giving the long-run supply curve a permanent sawtooth profile where marginal entrants earn strictly positive profits.

title: Markup and elasticity
bridge: Perfect competition assumed atomistic firms with zero pricing power who take market price as given. Markup and elasticity examines the opposite extreme: a single monopoly seller whose optimal price markup over marginal cost is governed entirely by the price elasticity of demand.
blurb: markup = 1/|elasticity| is exactly true at every optimum — and it is a statement about a single point. Two demand curves through that point set the same price to the last digit, and one passes half a cost increase through while the other passes two and a half times.

title: Monopolistic competition
bridge: Markup and elasticity analyzed a monopolist sheltered from rival varieties, while perfect competition assumed identical commodities. Monopolistic competition bridges both: differentiated brands compete for market share under free entry, but finite variety leaves firms operating with permanent excess capacity.
blurb: Every textbook result in monopolistic competition is an infinite-variety limit: firm scale falls short of the Dixit–Stiglitz benchmark by exactly 1/n, the equilibrium markup exceeds the continuum markup by 1/(σ(n − 1)), and the market produces (σ − 1)/σ varieties too many.

title: Cartels and the Prisoner's Dilemma
bridge: Monopolistic competition treated differentiated firms as non-collusive price-setters in a large market. Cartels and the Prisoner's Dilemma examines oligopoly with few players, where firms attempt to coordinate on monopoly output but outsiders capture a disproportionate free-rider windfall.
blurb: A merger of k of n Cournot firms is profitable only when k(n − k + 2)² < (n + 1)²; in a 5-firm market, a 4-firm cartel leaves member profits unchanged to the last cent while the lone outsider quadruples its earnings. Cartel instability is not just secret cheating — it is an overwhelming free-rider windfall.

title: Tragedy of the commons
bridge: Cartels demonstrated how strategic externalities across firms undermine collective discipline in output markets. Tragedy of the commons turns that external wedge onto open-access resources, where individual users equate average product rather than marginal product to cost, rapidly dissipating the shared rent.
blurb: With n users on an open-access resource, equilibrium equates average product to cost rather than marginal product, dissipating exactly ((n − 1)/n)² of the total resource rent. The second user alone destroys 25% of the maximum surplus, and half of all rent is gone by the fourth user.

title: Gini and the Lorenz curve
bridge: Tragedy of the commons showed how uncoordinated resource use destroys aggregate social rent. Gini and the Lorenz curve concludes Stage 1 Microeconomics by measuring how the resulting income and wealth are distributed across a population, and why a single summary index remains blind to distributional shape.
blurb: The Gini coefficient measures the average gap between two randomly chosen incomes relative to twice the mean, and 2·AUC − 1 is the exact same geometry applied to a ranking. Two credit scorecards with the identical Gini can differ by 14.4 percentage points of default capture in the top decile.

title: Measuring GDP
bridge: Gini and the Lorenz curve closed the microeconomics principles by measuring how income is shared out. Measuring GDP opens the macroeconomics principles by measuring how much there is to share, and shows that the minus sign in front of imports is a correction for foreign content rather than a cost.
blurb: GDP is C + I + G + X − M, and the minus sign is a correction, not a cost: an import changes GDP only through the home production it displaces, anywhere from none of its value to all of it, while the net-exports line in the release reads the same across that whole range.

title: Price indices
bridge: Measuring GDP added up a year's production in that year's prices. Price indices asks how to compare prices across years, and finds that a fixed basket overstates the rise in the cost of living by an amount that depends on how readily people substitute, which nobody observes.
blurb: A fixed basket overstates the cost of living by about half σ times the variance of the price changes: nothing when prices move together, quadratic in how far apart they move. Yet the Fisher index, built only from the two baskets people actually bought, lands on the true answer for every σ at once.

title: Unemployment flows
bridge: Price indices showed how a single number can hide the substitution behind it. Unemployment flows does the same for the unemployment rate, a stock fed by people losing jobs and people finding them, whose steady state depends only on the ratio of the two flows.
blurb: The unemployment rate depends only on the ratio of job finding to job loss, so doubling layoffs and halving hiring give exactly the same rate, unemployment can nearly double while layoffs fall, and the same 6% can mean two-month spells in one town and eleven-month spells in another.

title: Compound growth
bridge: Unemployment flows looked at how an economy uses the workers it has from month to month. Compound growth turns to the long run, where a one-point gap in growth rates doubles the gap in living standards in about seventy years, and asks what happens when growth is uncertain.
blurb: A one-point gap in growth rates doubles the gap in living standards in about seventy years. But the average growth rate isn't the rate you grew at, and with uncertain growth the typical path falls behind the expected one for ever: the share of paths above the expected level is exactly Φ(−σ√t/2).

title: Money creation
bridge: Compound growth dealt with real output over decades. Money creation turns to the money that output is bought with, following one loan through three banks' balance sheets to show where deposits come from and what the money multiplier really measures.
blurb: A bank that lends alone loses (1 − its share) of the loan in reserves, which is why bankers think deposits come first. Banks lending in step lose exactly nothing, so loans create deposits, and the money multiplier is a ratio that holds whichever way the causation runs.

title: Constrained choice
bridge: Money creation closed the macroeconomics principles with the banking system as a whole. Constrained choice opens the intermediate microeconomics by stepping down to a single person's decision, where an indifference curve meets a budget line, and asks what a pay rise does to how much someone chooses to work.
blurb: A pay rise makes free time dearer and makes you richer, and every course says theory cannot tell you which effect wins. For the utility function every course draws it does: they cancel to the last digit the arithmetic can carry, at every wage — and what actually shortened the working day was a subsistence floor getting out of the way, not one effect beating the other.

title: Nash equilibrium
bridge: Constrained choice resolved how a single optimizing individual behaves against fixed constraints. Nash equilibrium expands individual choice into multi-agent strategic interaction, where each player's optimal action depends on the anticipated choices of every rival.
blurb: One game in eight has no equilibrium you can find by checking cells. In those games your own behaviour is built entirely from the other player's payoffs — so raising a penalty does not reduce the thing it punishes, it buys less monitoring, at exactly the rate that leaves misconduct where it was.

title: Bargaining and the surplus
bridge: Nash equilibrium identified static equilibria in simultaneous games. Bargaining and the surplus studies dynamic bilateral negotiation over time, proving that relative patience and outside options dictate a unique division of economic surplus on the Pareto frontier.
blurb: Any point on the frontier beats no deal, and nothing in the picture picks one — until offers alternate, and then the model picks exactly one, built from the other side's impatience over both, with your outside option worth exactly nothing until it crosses the line.

title: Externalities
bridge: Bargaining and the surplus showed how two parties who can negotiate directly split the gains from a deal. Externalities brings in a party who is not at the table: when one side's action imposes a cost nobody prices, a bargain, a tax and a quota reach the same quantity and split the money differently, and only the regulator's uncertainty about costs makes the choice between a price and a quantity matter.
blurb: A tax, a quota and a bargain reach the same quantity and move the same money into different pockets, so the choice looks purely distributional — until the regulator is uncertain, and then the expected-loss ratio between price and quantity is the square of a slope ratio, crossing at exactly one.

title: Efficiency wages
bridge: Externalities assumed the costly action could be seen and measured, so a bargain, a tax or a quota could aim straight at it. Efficiency wages turns to an action nobody can see, a worker's effort: when effort cannot be observed, employers pay above the market-clearing wage so that losing the job hurts, which makes involuntary unemployment an equilibrium outcome.
blurb: The wage buys effort, and the cheapest effort sits where the effort elasticity is exactly one — a number labour demand never enters, which is why one worker and a thousand draw the same pay and the queue outside is the collateral, not the failure.

title: Isolation Forest
blurb: Anomalies are few, and they are different. Both of those make them easy to cut off from everything else — and that is the whole algorithm.

title: XGBoost
blurb: Why predict the answer when you can predict your own mistakes? How trees, gradients and shrinkage turn a sequence of simple rules into the default model for tabular data.

title: LightGBM
blurb: Bucket a column into 255 bins and the search for its best split stops being a scan over rows. It costs less than half a percent of the accuracy — and the speed does not come from where almost everyone says it does.

title: K-Means
blurb: Two moves, repeated until nothing changes. The algorithm always stops, it never makes things worse, and it is under no obligation whatsoever to be right.

title: Autoencoders
blurb: Squeeze data through a narrow layer and ask for it back, and a linear autoencoder rediscovers principal component analysis — in a basis nobody asked for, which it will never fix, because nothing in the loss can tell the difference.

title: Shapley Values
blurb: Three people, one fee, and no obvious way to split it. The answer game theory settled in 1953 turns out to be the answer to a question nobody was asking then: what did each feature contribute to this prediction?

title: SMOTE
blurb: The whole algorithm is one line: put a new minority point somewhere on the segment between two old ones. That line is a claim about the space between — where the claim is false, and what it was buying you anyway.

title: F1 Score
blurb: Maximising F1 on a validation set is the standard way to pick a classification threshold. The rule has a closed form, it is not about your problem, and it asserts a cost ratio nobody chose.

title: DBSCAN & HDBSCAN
blurb: Every value of eps you could try is one horizontal line drawn across the same tree. When the branches do not line up, none of them is right — not a hard search, an empty set — and HDBSCAN's answer is to stop cutting straight.

title: Population Stability Index
blurb: Every reading is how far the population moved plus (B−1)(1/N + 1/M), and the second term is there whether anything moved or not. The 0.10 and 0.25 lines ignore it — so on a small segment the traffic light is mostly reporting your sample size, and on a large one it cannot see a shift worth eight points of approval rate.
